hints: Count outer electrons first, carbon brings 4 crosses and oxygen brings 6 dots, and remember all 10 must appear with each atom ending with 8 around it.
walkthrough:
Picture what triple means for electrons**
Think of CO as two atoms sharing 6 electrons in the middle, that is 3 pairs. Each atom also keeps one lone pair to itself. That gives each atom 6 shared + 2 lone = 8 electrons, a full octet.

Place dots and crosses to show the dative bond**
Let crosses be carbon electrons and dots be oxygen electrons. Draw two shared pairs as dot plus cross, these are normal covalent bonds. Draw the third shared pair as dot plus dot, both from oxygen, this is the coordinate bond donated from O to C. Then give carbon its own lone pair of two crosses and oxygen its own lone pair of two dots.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram showing C triple bonded to O with one lone pair on each atom. Two shared pairs show one dot + one cross, the third shared pair shows two dots (dative from O). C has one lone pair of crosses, O has one lone pair of dots.

hints: Write $\Delta H$ = sum of bonds broken minus sum of bonds formed, and list what G contains: 2 C-C, 2 C-O, 10 C-H broken, while products form 6 C-H in $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$, 4 C-H in $\text{CH}_{4}$, 1 C-C, plus 1 $\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$.
Substitute the Table 3.1 values and $\Delta H = -7$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, then rearrange to isolate bond energy($\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$).
walkthrough:
Count bonds like an inventory**
Look at Fig 3.1 for G, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. You break 2 $\text{C-C}$, 2 $\text{C-O}$ and 10 $\text{C-H}$. In products you make ethane with 1 $\text{C-C}$ + 6 $\text{C-H}$, methane with 4 $\text{C-H}$, and CO with 1 $\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$. So total formed is 1 $\text{C-C}$, 10 $\text{C-H}$ and 1 $\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$.

Plug into the bond energy equation**
Remember breaking needs energy in (positive) and forming releases energy (subtracted): $$\Delta H = [2(350)+2(360)+10(410)] - [350+10(410)+BE(\text{C}\equiv\text{O})]$$ That is $$-7 = 5520 - 4450 - BE(\text{C}\equiv\text{O})$$ Rearranging gives $$BE(\text{C}\equiv\text{O}) = 5520 - 4450 + 7 = 1077\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Final answer: $$\Delta H = \Sigma(\text{bonds broken}) - \Sigma(\text{bonds formed})$$
$$-7 = [2(350) + 2(360) + 10(410)] - [10(410) + 350 + BE(\text{C}\equiv\text{O})]$$
bond energy ($\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$) = $1077$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall $K_{c}$ is products over reactants with each concentration raised to its balancing number, here all coefficients are 1.
Work out units by putting $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ in for each concentration and cancelling top against bottom.
walkthrough:
Build the fraction**
For $$\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{(g)} + \text{CO(g)} + \text{CH}_{4}\text{(g)}$$ put the three product concentrations multiplied together on top and the single reactant concentration below. No powers are needed because every balancing number is 1: $$K_{c} = \frac{[\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}][\text{CO}][\text{CH}_{4}]}{[\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}]}$$

Cancel units**
Each $[ ]$ has units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. So top gives $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{3}$ and bottom gives $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{1}$. Dividing leaves $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{2} = \text{mol}^{2}\text{dm}^{-6}$.

Final answer: $$K_{c} = \frac{[\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}][\text{CO}][\text{CH}_{4}]}{[\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}]}$$
units = $\text{mol}^{2}\text{dm}^{-6}$

hints: Compare the two $E_{a}$ values in Table 3.2, 143 versus 224 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, to decide what role $\text{I}_{2}$ plays.
Recall whether a catalyst changes the starting and finishing energies or only the route between them, and what that means for position of equilibrium and $K_{c}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the catalyst clue**
$E_{a}$ drops from $224$ to $143$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ when $\text{I}_{2}$ is present. Lower $E_{a}$ with the same overall reaction is the classic sign of a catalyst providing an alternative pathway.

Link catalyst to equilibrium**
A catalyst lowers $E_{a}$ for forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally and equilibrium is reached faster but with the same composition. Since $K_{c}$ depends only on equilibrium composition (and temperature, which is unchanged), $K_{c}$ shows no change.

Final answer: No change to $K_{c}$.
$\text{I}_{2}$ is a catalyst which lowers $E_{a}$ and speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so position of equilibrium is unchanged and $K_{c}$ is unchanged.

hints: Remember total number of molecules is fixed, so the area under the new curve must stay the same as the original.
Think how higher temperature shifts average energy and the spread, and what that does to peak height, peak position and the tail beyond $E_{a}$.
walkthrough:
Keep the start and area rules**
Every Boltzmann curve starts at the origin because no molecules have zero energy, and the total area under the curve equals the total number of molecules, which does not change. So your new curve must also start at (0,0) and enclose the same area.

Shift for higher temperature**
At $(T+100)^{\circ}\text{C}$ average energy is higher and energies are more spread out. Draw the peak lower and shifted to the right (higher energy). The curve should stay below the original around the peak, then cross over beyond the peak and stay above it out in the tail, showing many more molecules now have $E \ge E_{a}$.

Final answer: Curve starts at origin, peaks lower and to the right of original peak, with larger area beyond $E_{a}$. Curve does not cross original curve until beyond the original peak and stays above original at high energy.

hints: Compare the functional group in G, C-O-C, with what H must contain since H turns acidified dichromate from orange to green.
walkthrough:
Compare what can react**
G is an ether, C-O-C, and stays orange with acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$, so it is not oxidised. H turns orange to green, so H is oxidised and must contain a different functional group, an alcohol -OH, but with the same molecular formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. Same formula, different functional group means functional group isomerism.

hints: Both H and J turn dichromate green so both are alcohols with the same carbon skeleton, think what can still differ if the functional group and skeleton are the same.
walkthrough:
Narrow down H versus J**
Both H and J are straight chain molecules oxidised by dichromate, so both are straight chain alcohols. They have different boiling points, 117 and 98 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. The only difference left is where the -OH sits on the chain, which is positional isomerism.

hints: Use the straight chain clue plus the formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ to sketch the two straight chain alcohol skeletons.
Recall boiling point falls with more branching or with secondary versus primary -OH due to weaker hydrogen bonding packing, so the higher boiling point (117) fits the primary alcohol.
Name straight chain alcohols by numbering the -OH carbon to give the lowest number.
walkthrough:
Draw the two straight chain options**
With four carbons in a row you can only put -OH on carbon 1 or carbon 2 (carbon 3 mirrors carbon 2). So sketch $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$.

Assign H and J by boiling point**
Primary alcohols pack and hydrogen bond slightly more effectively than secondary alcohols, giving a higher boiling point. H boils at 117 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ so H is the primary alcohol, butan-1-ol. J boils at 98 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ so J is the secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol.

Give systematic names**
Number from the end nearest the -OH. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ has -OH on C1, butan-1-ol. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$ has -OH on C2, butan-2-ol.

Final answer: H: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, butan-1-ol
J: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$, butan-2-ol

hints: Orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH tells you K has a C=O of an aldehyde or ketone, then ask which of those also gives a silver mirror with Tollens.
Build the displayed formula for a 3 carbon aldehyde, showing every atom and bond as C-C-C with C=O and C-H on the end carbon.
walkthrough:
Combine the two test results**
Orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine means a carbonyl compound, aldehyde or ketone. Silver mirror with Tollens means it is oxidised easily, which only aldehydes do (ketones give no reaction). So K is an aldehyde with formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}$.

Draw propanal fully displayed**
The only 3 carbon aldehyde is propanal, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$. Draw it displayed: $\text{H}_{3}\text{C-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}$ with a double bond $\text{C=O}$ and single bond $\text{C-H}$ on the last carbon, showing every C-H, C-C and C=O bond explicitly.
Final answer: K is propanal: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$ shown as displayed formula with all bonds: C-C-C backbone, $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-H}$ on carbon 1 and all C-H bonds shown.
